chief_complaint: bloating, crampy abdominal pain, vomiting, no gas
hpi_details: A 29-year-old male presents to the clinic with 1 day of crampy, colicky abdominal pain, bloating, and vomiting, with inability to pass gas or stool. He had an open appendectomy several years ago.
ideas: thinks it might be a bowel blockage (small bowel obstruction)
concerns: He is worried that his intestine is going to burst from the pressure and require another large open abdominal surgery.
expectations: He hopes to receive a strong prescription laxative or an enema to flush out the blockage and relieve the nausea.

investigation_events.title: STAT small-bowel obstruction results
investigation_events.availability_message: The STAT small-bowel obstruction results are now available; nasogastric decompression, IV fluids, and surgical consultation should not be delayed.

results.test: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
results.value: Dilated small-bowel loops with an adhesive transition point near the prior appendectomy site and collapsed distal bowel; no closed-loop obstruction, pneumatosis, or free air

clinical_knowledge.topic: Small Bowel Obstruction (adhesions) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Small Bowel Obstruction (adhesions) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes NPO status, IV hydration, nasogastric tube decompression, and urgent surgical consultation to identify strangulation requiring emergency surgery, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: bloating, crampy abdominal pain, vomiting, no gas

Key HPI features: A 29-year-old male presents to the clinic with 1 day of crampy, colicky abdominal pain, bloating, and vomiting, with inability to pass gas or stool. He had an open appendectomy several years ago.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: Temp 37.2C, HR 100, BP 116/74. Abdomen distended and tympanitic with high-pitched, hyperactive bowel sounds; no rebound, guarding, or peritonitis. Well-healed lower midline surgical scar. Abdominal X-ray series shows dilated small bowel loops with air-fluid levels.
Relevant background/PMH: Open appendectomy several years ago
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Small Bowel Obstruction (adhesions).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Ileus without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Fever or constant severe pain — suggests strangulation.
management_principles: Keep NPO, insert nasogastric tube for decompression, and start IV hydration with electrolyte correction
Order abdominal X-ray series and CT abdomen/pelvis to confirm the diagnosis and exclude strangulation
Obtain urgent general surgery consultation; escalate to emergency surgery if signs of strangulation, peritonitis, or clinical deterioration develop
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

Chief Complaint: bloating, crampy abdominal pain, vomiting, no gas

A 29-year-old male presents to the clinic with 1 day of crampy, colicky abdominal pain, bloating, and vomiting, with inability to pass gas or stool. He had an open appendectomy several years ago.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: Temp 37.2C, HR 100, BP 116/74. Abdomen distended and tympanitic with high-pitched, hyperactive bowel sounds; no rebound, guarding, or peritonitis. Well-healed lower midline surgical scar. Abdominal X-ray series shows dilated small bowel loops with air-fluid levels.
reference_soap.assessment: Small bowel obstruction, likely secondary to post-surgical adhesions, without current signs of strangulation.
reference_soap.plan: Keep NPO, insert nasogastric tube for decompression, and start IV hydration with electrolyte correction. Order abdominal X-ray series and CT abdomen/pelvis to confirm the diagnosis and exclude strangulation. Obtain urgent general surgery consultation; escalate to emergency surgery if signs of strangulation, peritonitis, or clinical deterioration develop.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Small Bowel Obstruction
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Small Bowel Obstruction
Implement evidence-based management plan: NPO, IV hydration, nasogastric tube decompression

teaching.one_liner: Post-surgical scar tissue narrows the small bowel, causing bloating, crampy pain, vomiting, and inability to pass gas.
red_flags: Fever or constant severe pain — suggests strangulation

must_ask.say: Have you had any abdominal surgery in the past?
Does the pain come in cramping waves?
Can you pass gas or have a bowel movement?

history.answer: My stomach has been cramping and bloating since yesterday, and I keep throwing up and haven't been able to pass any gas or stool.
It started about twenty-four hours ago and came on fairly quickly, and it has been getting worse over the course of yesterday and today.
The pain is mostly around my belly button and all across the middle of my belly, and it hasn't moved anywhere else.
No, it stays right in the center of my stomach and does not radiate to my back, shoulder, or groin.
It comes in waves of sharp, crampy spasms that peak intensely and then ease up for several minutes before returning.
During the spasms it gets up to about a seven out of ten, but between the spasms it stays at a dull ache around three or four.
Trying to eat or drink anything triggers immediate cramps and vomiting, and lying curled on my side gives only minimal relief.
No, I have never had severe abdominal pain or cramps like this before.
I have vomited four or five times since yesterday, starting with undigested food and now just greenish-yellow fluid, with no blood.
I have not been able to pass any stool or even a little bit of gas since yesterday morning.
Yes, my abdomen has become visibly swollen and tight, like an inflated balloon.
No, I have not had any fever, shivering, or chills.
No, my eyes and skin are not yellow, and my urine has not been dark.
No, urination feels completely normal with no pain, burning, frequent trips, or blood.
I felt a little lightheaded when I stood up earlier because I haven't kept anything down, but I have not fainted.
No chest pain, chest pressure, or shortness of breath at all.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 116/74 mmHg, heart rate is 100 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation is 98% on room air, and temperature is 37.2°C.
The patient appears uncomfortable and fatigued, lying still with intermittent distress during cramping episodes.
The abdomen is visibly distended with a well-healed surgical scar in the lower abdomen from a prior appendectomy, and no visible peristalsis or skin discoloration.
High-pitched, hyperactive tinkling bowel sounds and rushes are heard throughout all four quadrants.
Diffuse tympany is present on percussion across the distended abdomen with no shifting dullness.
Mild diffuse tenderness is elicited on palpation across the periumbilical region without involuntary guarding or abdominal rigidity.
No rebound tenderness or peritoneal signs are present.
Murphy sign is negative with no tenderness in the right upper quadrant during deep inspiration.
McBurney point is non-tender, and psoas and obturator signs are negative.
No palpable bulges, masses, or tenderness are noted in the bilateral inguinal or femoral canals, and no umbilical hernia is seen.
Empty rectal vault with normal sphincter tone, no palpable mass, and no gross blood on the examining glove.
